facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Leverage fell sharply and has since stopped improving. Total debt at carrying value dropped from USD 31,660 million at FY2023 to USD 24,988 million at FY2025 while derived EBITDA rose from USD 6,882 million to USD 7,652 million, taking total debt to EBITDA from 4.60x to 3.27x. Since then debt has risen to USD 26,398 million as aircraft financings of 4.6 billion outran repayments, and total debt to EBITDA is 3.31x for the twelve months to 2026-09-30. Net debt to EBITDA of 2.48x looks level with FY2025 at 2.49x, but the last twelve months include net special credits of USD 756 million, which reflect aircraft sale-leaseback gains recorded in 2026, and without them net leverage is 2.74x against 2.41x. For creditors, the improvement came mainly from repaying debt, with payments of long-term debt, finance leases and other financial liabilities of USD 10,138 million in FY2024 and USD 4,771 million in FY2025 against issuance of USD 6,139 million and USD 578 million, and the next test is whether earnings carry the added fleet debt without special credits. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 95–96, 128; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4, 16–21; calculation C15; calculation C16; calculation C19

facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Cash interest cover strengthened as expensive debt was repaid. EBITDA covered cash interest paid 3.72 times in FY2023, 5.37 times in FY2024 and 5.75 times in FY2025, while interest expense fell from USD 1,956 million to USD 1,373 million. The last twelve months cash figure cannot be built because the quarterly reports omit cash paid for interest, so the accrued-expense cover of 5.88 times is shown as a proxy only. The strongest contrary reading is that new aircraft debt at floating rates, about 1.4% above the benchmark, adds interest that the earlier years did not carry; interest expense for the nine months already ran at USD 1,029 million against USD 1,048 million a year earlier, so the effect is not yet visible. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 95, 97; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3, 17–18; calculation C17; calculation C20

facts.label: Financial interpretation
facts.text: Cash conversion has weakened. Free cash flow, operating cash flow less capital expenditure, was USD 3,830 million in FY2024 and USD 2,557 million in FY2025, and USD 1,116 million for the twelve months to 2026-09-30, or 0.14 of EBITDA against 0.33 in FY2025. Capital expenditure rose to USD 7,044 million over the latest twelve months from USD 5,874 million as aircraft deliveries continued, and operating cash flow was held back by a one-off flight attendant ratification payment. The mechanism is that fleet investment is outrunning internally generated cash and being met with new secured debt, which raises leverage unless EBITDA grows with it. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a benign view is the cost trend: reported nine-month operating income rose 6.4% only because of USD 749 million of special credits, mostly gains on aircraft sale-leasebacks, while the underlying measure fell 22.37% and the third-quarter margin slipped to 8.09% from 9.16%. A further fuel rise that fares cannot recover, or a demand slowdown with the same cost base, would cut free cash flow that already fell in 2026, and the unhedged position gives creditors no buffer. facts.label: Bottom line
facts.text: United's credit profile is sound but no longer improving: scale, liquidity and lower debt support creditors, while an unhedged fuel shock, higher labor cost and heavy aircraft spending have cut margin and free cash flow, so risk lies in cash conversion, not liquidity. Total debt is 3.31x EBITDA and net debt 2.48x, or 2.74x without special credits, and free cash flow fell to USD 1,116 million over twelve months. facts.label: Company description
facts.text: The strategic shift that matters for creditors is the United Next fleet plan, which commits the company to several hundred new aircraft by 2034 and to the financing that goes with them, while the 2025 and 2026 history is one of debt repayment, a larger regional supplier merger and a labor reset. The newest filing covers the quarter ended 2026-09-30, which is 49 days before the as-of date, and was signed 28 days before it. Its disclosure of an amended revolving credit facility dated 2026-10-16 is a subsequent event that the quarter-end balance sheet does not reflect.

spans.text: ## Request

Financial foundation for United Airlines Holdings, Inc. as of 2026-11-18 on the credit snapshot pathway. Scope is the consolidated holding-company statements for FY2023 to FY2025 and the nine months to 2026-09-30, carrying-value debt, liquidity, derived EBITDA and a last-twelve-months build, with the 2026-10-16 revolving credit facility amendment shown as a subsequent event.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Leverage has stopped improving: for the twelve months to 2026-09-30 total debt is 3.31x EBITDA, up from 3.27x at FY2025, and net debt is 2.48x, level with 2.49x; creditors should read the flat net figure as 2.74x once net special credits are removed. EBITDA is derived because the issuer states none, and it includes net special credits of USD 756 million.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 95–97; calculation C15; calculation C16; calculation C19

Free cash flow fell to USD 1,116 million over those twelve months from USD 2,557 million in FY2025 as capital expenditure rose, and debt grew to USD 26,398 million. Liquidity is large, with USD 14,653 million of cash and short-term investments and USD 3,000 million of undrawn revolver commitments, which the October 2026 amendment raises to USD 5,000 million.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4, 16; calculation C21; calculation C22
Cash interest paid is printed only for full years, so interest cover on a cash basis is not calculable for the latest twelve months; on interest expense, EBITDA covers interest 5.88 times.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 97; calculation C20

### Financial interpretation

Leverage fell sharply and has since stopped improving. Total debt at carrying value dropped from USD 31,660 million at FY2023 to USD 24,988 million at FY2025 while derived EBITDA rose from USD 6,882 million to USD 7,652 million, taking total debt to EBITDA from 4.60x to 3.27x. Since then debt has risen to USD 26,398 million as aircraft financings of 4.6 billion outran repayments, and total debt to EBITDA is 3.31x for the twelve months to 2026-09-30. Net debt to EBITDA of 2.48x looks level with FY2025 at 2.49x, but the last twelve months include net special credits of USD 756 million, which reflect aircraft sale-leaseback gains recorded in 2026, and without them net leverage is 2.74x against 2.41x. For creditors, the improvement came mainly from repaying debt, with payments of long-term debt, finance leases and other financial liabilities of USD 10,138 million in FY2024 and USD 4,771 million in FY2025 against issuance of USD 6,139 million and USD 578 million, and the next test is whether earnings carry the added fleet debt without special credits.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 95–96, 128; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4, 16–21; calculation C15; calculation C16; calculation C19

Cash interest cover strengthened as expensive debt was repaid. EBITDA covered cash interest paid 3.72 times in FY2023, 5.37 times in FY2024 and 5.75 times in FY2025, while interest expense fell from USD 1,956 million to USD 1,373 million. The last twelve months cash figure cannot be built because the quarterly reports omit cash paid for interest, so the accrued-expense cover of 5.88 times is shown as a proxy only. The strongest contrary reading is that new aircraft debt at floating rates, about 1.4% above the benchmark, adds interest that the earlier years did not carry; interest expense for the nine months already ran at USD 1,029 million against USD 1,048 million a year earlier, so the effect is not yet visible.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 95, 97; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3, 17–18; calculation C17; calculation C20

Cash conversion has weakened. Free cash flow, operating cash flow less capital expenditure, was USD 3,830 million in FY2024 and USD 2,557 million in FY2025, and USD 1,116 million for the twelve months to 2026-09-30, or 0.14 of EBITDA against 0.33 in FY2025. Capital expenditure rose to USD 7,044 million over the latest twelve months from USD 5,874 million as aircraft deliveries continued, and operating cash flow was held back by a one-off flight attendant ratification payment. The mechanism is that fleet investment is outrunning internally generated cash and being met with new secured debt, which raises leverage unless EBITDA grows with it.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 97; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4, 19–21; calculation C21; calculation C11; calculation C12

Liquidity is ample against near-term maturities but depends on customer-funded float. ## Gaps

- EBITDA is not stated by the issuer for any period, so EBITDA (Reported) is derived from operating income and depreciation and amortization for every income statement column and for the last twelve months to 2026-09-30; it includes special charges and credits and cannot be compared with an issuer or covenant EBITDA. Severity Medium. Action: obtain the earnings releases with the issuer reconciliations.

- Cash paid for interest and for income taxes is not printed for the nine months of 2025 and 2026, so cash interest cover for the last twelve months to 2026-09-30 is not calculable and the interest cover chart has no figure for that period. Severity Medium. Action: obtain the full interim cash flow statements.

- The condensed interim cash flow statements print only the operating total, so thirteen operating-activity lines, including the movements in advance ticket sales and frequent flyer deferred revenue, are not supplied for the nine months of 2025 and 2026. Severity Low. Action: obtain the full interim cash flow statements.
- The FY2023 statement prints a dash for repurchases of common stock; it is kept as a missing value, not zero. Severity Low. Action: none needed unless a share count roll-forward is required.

- Net Cash Change is not supplied for FY2025 and for the nine months of 2025 because the printed activity totals differ from the printed net change by 1 million (FY2025 minus 2864 against minus 2865; nine months 2025 minus 2076 against minus 2075), which the filing attributes to rounding. Severity Low. Action: none; the opening and closing cash balances are printed.

- Income statement and balance sheet subtotals differ from the sum of their printed lines by 1 or 2 million in several columns (for example FY2025 operating expense lines add to 54357 against 54356 printed), and the maturity ladder adds to 23115 against 23116 printed; printed totals are kept. Severity Low. Action: none.

- The debt note at 2026-09-30 prints a principal ladder and carrying value only, with no instrument table, so the instrument rows are at 2025-12-31 with 2026 movements shown separately and the debt stack is drawn at 2025-12-31. This restricts composition, security and maturity by instrument at the latest date. Severity Medium. Action: obtain the debt schedule at 2026-09-30.

- Finance leases and other financial liabilities at 2026-09-30 are not itemised; 3434 of the debt captions is obtained by difference from the debt note carrying value, and the reconciling item in the principal to carrying value table rests on it. Severity Medium. Action: obtain the lease and other financial liability schedule at 2026-09-30.

- The undrawn amount under the revolving credit facility at 2023-12-31 is not printed in the supplied filings, so the liquidity chart has no undrawn figure for FY2023. Severity Low. Action: obtain the FY2023 annual report.

- Annual amortisation, interest floors and the obligor or guarantor scope are not stated for several instruments, and the carrying value is printed only for the debt table total, so those cells in the debt instrument register are not supplied. Severity Medium. Action: obtain the credit agreements, indentures and debt schedule.

- Neither the security nor the rank of the 2029 and 2031 senior notes issued in 2026 is stated, and no source states the priority among the secured instruments, which rest on different collateral; the debt stack therefore omits the two notes and groups the secured instruments under one rank. Severity Medium. Action: obtain the indentures.
- No EBITDA bridge is stated because the issuer reports no adjusted EBITDA and no add-backs. Severity Low. Action: none unless an issuer measure is later supplied.

- The balance of letters of credit and surety bonds is printed only at 2025-12-31 (USD 502 million), and the minimum liquidity levels in the card-processing agreements are not quantified, so liquidity net of letters of credit cannot be updated to 2026-09-30. Severity Medium. Action: obtain the current schedule of letters of credit and the processor terms.

- The issuer reports one segment, so no segment schedule is written and no segment sum is stated; revenue by type is in the income statement and revenue by region is in the filings. Severity Low. Action: none.

- The reported collateral coverage ratio and the appraised collateral value are printed in no source, so covenant headroom for the minimum collateral coverage ratio of 1.6 to 1.0 and the minimum liquidity of USD 2,000 million is not calculable and none is inferred. Severity Medium. Action: obtain the compliance certificates or collateral appraisal.

- The revolving credit facility amendment of 2026-10-16 falls after the latest balance sheet and is kept out of every period figure; any pro forma liquidity view must be labelled as such. Severity Low. Action: report beside, not inside, quarter-end figures.

- The holding company and its operating subsidiary file separate statements that differ slightly, for example nine-month 2026 operating cash flow of 6874 against 6754; the holding company figures are used and the subsidiary figures are not extracted. Severity Low. Action: extract the subsidiary statements if a subsidiary view is needed.

spans.text: ## Request

Business, ownership and governance review of United Airlines Holdings, Inc. as of 2026-11-18 on the credit snapshot pathway. Scope is the operating model, ownership and control, capital allocation and sponsor-type behaviour, the 2026 financing and investment transactions and the dated event history, read from the five supplied filings and the source readiness review, with no external sources.
## Sources

No external sources were used.
## Findings
### Bottom line

United's credit risk is operating, not owner-driven: no controlling holder is disclosed, no dividend is paid and the loyalty business carries no secured debt, so creditors bear airline-cycle and fuel risk rather than extraction risk. In the nine months to 2026-09-30 fuel expense rose USD 4,520 million (53.35%) and operating income before special items fell 22.37% to USD 2,790 million, while reported operating income rose only because of USD 749 million of special credits.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 66; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21; calculation C6; calculation C7

The credit case therefore rests on pricing power against fuel and labor costs and on aircraft financing, because the revolver, the term loan and the 2029 senior secured notes share one collateral pool of route authorities, slots and terminal rights, and capital spending is rising.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; calculation C8; calculation C15
### Key findings

Ownership creates no identified sponsor risk: the shares are listed on Nasdaq, no holder is identified as controlling, the Treasury warrants issued in the pandemic were all exercised by March 2025, and the only other equity security outstanding is two junior preferred shares whose rights the filings read do not describe. The tax benefits preservation plan that deters any buyer from crossing 4.9% of the shares expires on 2026-12-04, after the as-of date, and the filings do not say it will be renewed.

The business is a scale network carrier with diversified geography but one core product: passenger revenue was 90.47% of FY2025 revenue and domestic revenue 59.28%, so earnings follow U.S. air travel demand and fares more than any second business. Cargo was 3.01% and other operating revenue 6.52%, most of it loyalty partner income.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 71; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 110; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 114; calculation C1; calculation C3; calculation C18

Loyalty is a real strength and prepayments are a real obligation: partner agreements, led by the co-brand card with JPMorgan Chase, produced about USD 3.2 billion of FY2025 revenue and grew 12.50% in the nine months to USD 2.7 billion, and no debt is now secured on the loyalty assets. Against that, customer prepayments of USD 18,637 million are 1.27x cash and short-term investments of USD 14,653 million, so a drop in bookings or a processor demand for reserves would reach liquidity quickly.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 138; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10; calculation C12; calculation C13; calculation C18

Fuel is the largest swing cost and is not hedged: it took 27.87% of nine-month operating expense against 21.00% a year earlier, at an average USD 3.65 per gallon against USD 2.43, the company does not hedge fuel and the filings give no price sensitivity. Fares have recovered much of it, with total revenue per seat mile up 11.9% on capacity up only 2.7%, but operating margin before special items still fell from 8.23% to 5.56%.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 26; calculation C6; calculation C8

Labor is the largest cost line and is repricing upward: 83% of employees are represented by unions, salaries and related costs grew 8.28% in the nine months, and flight attendants ratified a five-year agreement in May 2026 with a USD 740 million ratification payment on 2026-09-15. The annual report also lists several other groups whose agreements were already open for amendment and states that negotiations are active with all of them.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 19; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ual-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21; calculation C10; calculation C11

Shareholder distributions have been modest and creditor-aligned so far: no dividend is paid, repurchases of USD 637 million in FY2025 were 24.91% of free cash flow and fell to USD 27 million in the nine months to 2026-09-30, and the MileagePlus debt was repaid in 2024 and 2025. In 2026 the direction on debt reversed, with nine-month borrowing of USD 6,698 million above repayments of USD 5,541 million to fund aircraft.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 66; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 75; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 78; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 96; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation C14; calculation C19

Capital spending is the main call on cash: nine-month capital expenditure rose 29.37% to USD 5,154 million, nine-month free cash flow fell to USD 1,720 million from USD 3,161 million, and the annual report guides 2026 adjusted capital expenditure to less than USD 8.0 billion because of aircraft delivery delays. The firm order book that runs to 2034 fell by 82 aircraft over three quarters, so the commitment is long and largely contractual.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 63; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 76; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 77; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 30; calculation C14; calculation C15; calculation C16

Related-party exposure is small against the business but structural: United holds minority stakes in the regional carriers that fly under its capacity contracts, pays them about USD 1.1 billion a year, and committed financial contributions, whose amount is not stated, to the 2025 merger of Mesa and Republic in return for an additional stake that took its holding in Republic to about 22%. These contracts are described as ordinary-course and are not shown to leak value to a shareholder.

Reporting quality is sound: the auditor issued unqualified opinions on the statements and on internal control over financial reporting, the single critical audit matter concerns the China route authority intangible asset, and disclosure controls were concluded effective at 2026-09-30. Reporting follows the quarterly cycle with no restatement or waiver described.

The shared collateral pool is the main structural point for unsecured creditors: route authorities, slots and terminal rights secure the revolver, the term loan and the 2029 senior secured notes on a shared senior basis, a substantial part of the aircraft is also pledged, and the revolver was enlarged from USD 3.0 billion to USD 5.0 billion on 2026-10-16, after the latest balance sheet. Owned aircraft are 89.87% of the mainline fleet, but owned does not mean unencumbered.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 63; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 38–39; calculation C16
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a benign view is the cost trend: reported nine-month operating income rose 6.4% only because of USD 749 million of special credits, mostly gains on aircraft sale-leasebacks, while the underlying measure fell 22.37% and the third-quarter margin slipped to 8.09% from 9.16%. A further fuel rise that fares cannot recover, or a demand slowdown with the same cost base, would cut free cash flow that already fell in 2026, and the unhedged position gives creditors no buffer.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ual-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 25; calculation C7; calculation C8; calculation C20

The view that owner behaviour is not a risk would change if a holder crossed 5% after the preservation plan lapses, if repurchases resumed at the FY2025 pace while capital spending rises, if secured debt were again raised on the loyalty assets, or if the revolver were drawn for distributions. The remaining USD 755 million repurchase authorisation and the loyalty assets that no longer secure debt show the capacity exists, though use of either is not yet documented.
### Limitations

- The proxy statement is not supplied, so board composition, independence, committee structure and holders above 5% are not established; the conclusion that no holder controls the company rests on the filings naming none, and a large holder or voting arrangement would overturn it.

- The credit agreements and indentures are not supplied, so capacity to pay dividends, repurchase shares, add secured debt or move assets cannot be measured; the low governance risk rests on documented behaviour and would be reassessed once the covenant package is read.

- The filings report one segment and give no customer, route or hub profitability, so the claim that revenue is diversified rests on the split by region and by revenue type alone and hub concentration cannot be tested.

- The filings describe no fuel hedge and give no price sensitivity, so the estimate that fares have recovered much of the fuel increase rests on nine-month unit revenue changes and not on a stated pass-through, and it could reverse if demand softens.

- Loyalty partner income is disclosed only as rounded totals with no split of the co-brand card agreement, its term or minimum commitments, so the durability of the largest non-ticket income and the financing value of the loyalty assets that no longer secure debt are not established.
### Company and operating model
| Item | What the filings state | Why it matters to creditors | Source |

| Network and hubs | Hub-and-spoke network with hubs at Chicago, Denver, Houston, Los Angeles, Newark, San Francisco, Washington Dulles and Guam, serving six continents with the regional carriers | Scale supports origin-and-destination traffic, but one hub failure spreads across the network; Newark air traffic problems in 2025 and the late 2025 government shutdown forced schedule cuts | 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 4; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 38 |

| Group structure | UAL is a holding company; United Airlines, Inc. supplies nearly 100% of revenues and expenses and approximately the entire balance of assets, liabilities and operating cash flow | Cash and operating claims sit in the subsidiary; holding company notes depend on the subsidiary guarantee | 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 4 |

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The 2026 financing was a refinancing plus aircraft borrowing, not a shareholder distribution: on 2026-02-02 and 2026-02-06 the holding company issued USD 1,000 million each of senior notes due 2031 and 2029, both at par and guaranteed by the operating subsidiary, and on 2026-02-24 the operating subsidiary redeemed all USD 2,000 million of its senior secured notes due 2026. The filings do not state whether the new notes are secured or how they rank against the term loan and the secured notes.

The term loan was repriced on 2026-02-03 by Amendment No. 4, which cut the margin from 2.00% to 1.75% on Term SOFR loans and from 1.00% to 0.75% on other market-rate loans; the filings state no consideration given for the change. In the nine months to 2026-09-30 the operating subsidiary also borrowed USD 4.6 billion secured on aircraft, maturing between 2029 and 2038 at Term SOFR plus an average margin of 1.4%, and made USD 4.9 billion of debt payments, including a USD 0.6 billion partial prepayment on 2026-06-23 of the USD 1.5 billion Treasury payroll support note due 2030.

After the latest balance sheet, on 2026-10-16, the revolving credit facility was amended and restated: commitments rose from USD 3.0 billion to USD 5.0 billion, maturity moved from 2029-02-15 to 2031-10-16 and the margins were lowered, with no borrowing outstanding at the date of the report. The facility is secured by route authorities, slots and terminal rights that also secure the term loan and the 2029 senior secured notes, and its lenders may require prepayment if a change of control occurs and the lender accepts a change of control offer. Figures at 2026-09-30 in this review do not include it.

No purchase of an operating business and no sponsor transaction is described in the filings read. The equity-type transactions were investments: financial contributions to the merger of Mesa and Republic completed on 2025-11-25, whose amount is not stated, in exchange for 2,744,348 additional Republic shares received on 2026-02-03, and a USD 100 million subscription for Azul depositary shares agreed on 2026-02-17 that left United with 8.6% of Azul at 2026-09-30.

Fundamental credit synthesis of United Airlines Holdings, Inc. as of 2026-11-18 on the credit snapshot pathway. Scope is the business, financial profile, downside path and monitoring for the holding company group, drawn from the five supplied filings and the three earlier analyses, with no external sources.

## Findings
### Bottom line

United's credit profile is sound but no longer improving: scale, liquidity and lower debt support creditors, while an unhedged fuel shock, higher labor cost and heavy aircraft spending have cut margin and free cash flow, so risk lies in cash conversion, not liquidity. Total debt is 3.31x EBITDA and net debt 2.48x, or 2.74x without special credits, and free cash flow fell to USD 1,116 million over twelve months. Cash and short-term investments of USD 14,653 million cover principal due through 2029 1.52 times with no free cash flow, so the main downside is fuel staying above fares until the 2029 maturities must be refinanced.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against caution is pricing power: revenue rose 14.84% on capacity growth of 2.7%, unit revenue rose 11.9%, management states that its long-term outlook is positive because it expects demand to stay strong, and three agencies upgraded the company in 2025. If fuel falls back toward the USD 2.43 a gallon of the prior-year nine months while fares hold, the underlying margin would recover quickly because fuel is the swing cost, and the view would move to stable or improving.

### Limitations

- No peer filings, rating agency reports or market prices are supplied, so the judgement that the business profile is stronger than the leverage profile is not benchmarked against comparable airlines, and the rating trajectory rests on the company's own statements.

- The downside arithmetic holds volume, prices and all other costs at latest levels and ignores fare, capacity and capital spending responses, so it measures exposure and is not a forecast; a faster response would shrink the cash burn shown.

- Maturity coverage uses the principal ladder for long-term debt agreements only, which excludes finance leases and other financial liabilities and any payments on them, so the coverage of principal due through 2029 is overstated by an amount that is not established.

- No forward model or management plan beyond the 2026 capital expenditure guidance is supplied, so the outlook and the timing of the 2029 refinancing are read from disclosed commitments and not from projected cash flow.

### Company description

United is a hub-based network airline whose cash flow depends on passenger revenue, which was 90.47% of FY2025 revenue, with 59.28% earned in the domestic market and 40.72% in Atlantic, Pacific and Latin American markets. Cargo, loyalty partner income and ancillary fees add diversification of source but not of cycle, so earnings follow U.S. air travel demand, fares and fuel; tickets are sold at most twelve months ahead, so revenue visibility is short and the credit rests on liquidity and network scale rather than on contracted revenue.

### Cost structure and margin resilience

Costs are largely fixed in the short run: labor and fuel together are 53.43% of FY2025 operating expense, regional carriers are paid fixed-fee rates with USD 18.7 billion of estimated future payments, and firm aircraft orders carry material liabilities if modified. Margin can be defended only through fares and capacity: unit revenue less unit cost before special items fell 24.39% in the nine months, so cost inflation has so far outrun pricing at the margin even though revenue per seat mile rose.

### Porter's Five Forces

Rivalry is intense and pressures margin: the industry competes on routes, fares, capacity and loyalty, consolidation and immunized joint businesses reshape competitors, and the company states that it often has to match discounted fares to keep traffic. That limits the pass-through of cost increases and is why a fuel shock lands on margin first.

The threat of new entrants is moderate: any fit U.S. carrier may fly domestic routes, but slots, gates and airport infrastructure at the hubs are constrained, and the company's route authorities, slots and terminal rights are collateral for its secured debt, which supports their value to lenders.

Substitutes matter for short-haul and business travel: surface travel replaces short flights and videoconferencing replaces trips when conditions weaken, so a fall in business and premium travel would hit revenue first, which raises the cyclicality of cash flow.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ual-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 36

Buyer power is limited for consumers individually but real in aggregate: tickets are sold through the company's own channels and through agencies and online agencies, a legacy distribution cost remains, and the largest partner income depends on one co-brand card agreement whose terms are not disclosed.

Supplier power is high: substantially all aircraft and engines come from Boeing and Airbus and a limited number of engine suppliers, delivery delays and tariffs can raise cost or force older aircraft to stay in service, and the labor force is largely unionized under the Railway Labor Act, so suppliers and unions both set cost.
### PEST analysis

Political and regulatory factors are material: the FAA can restrict capacity at hubs, a federal government shutdown forced schedule cuts at about 40 airports in late 2025, tariffs on aircraft and parts could raise fleet cost, and labor agreements are negotiated under federal law with open amendable dates. Each of these acts on revenue or cost without any offset in the company's control, so they raise the volatility of cash flow.

Economic factors are the dominant driver: fuel prices rose with Middle East conflicts in 2026, demand follows economic strength, and floating-rate debt ties interest cost to market rates. Social and technological factors, such as customer service performance and system outages, are not primary credit drivers on the materials supplied.
### SWOT

The strengths are liquidity and committed facilities that cover principal due through 2029, a hub network with scale and loyalty income that does not move with fuel, lower debt than at FY2023 with rating upgrades in 2025, and loyalty assets that no longer secure debt.

### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over 12 to 24 months the headwinds are fuel at or above the third-quarter level of USD 3.90 a gallon, labor resets under agreements still open, and aircraft financing that adds debt, while the tailwinds are strong demand that management expects to persist, a revolver raised to USD 5.0 billion that extends to 2031, and principal due of only USD 2,318 million over the next 15 months. Free cash flow is the observable that decides whether leverage resumes falling.

### Qualitative downside scenario

The initiating condition is fuel staying at the third-quarter price of USD 3.90 a gallon for a further twelve months while fare gains stall, which on twelve-month volume adds USD 2,531 million of fuel expense, 31.77% of EBITDA. The first operational break is margin: EBITDA would fall to about USD 5,436 million, free cash flow would turn to a burn of USD 1,415 million, and total debt to EBITDA would rise to 4.86x with debt unchanged.

Liquidity absorbs it comfortably over a year, with cash and short-term investments covering the burn and the next 15 months of principal 3.93 times, and the amended revolver, a subsequent event, adds committed capacity of USD 5.0 billion that the ratio does not count. The pressure point is the refinancing: over three years the same burn plus principal due through 2029 would use almost all cash, 1.06 times covered, so resilience then depends on refinancing the 2029 principal, on market access at BB+ and Ba1, and on management levers such as capacity cuts, fare and fee increases, the timing of capital spending and no repurchases.

The primary downside path is a prolonged fuel price above fares and rising labor cost that turns free cash flow negative and lifts leverage ahead of the 2029 maturities, with the shared collateral pool leaving unsecured creditors exposed if market access closes. The scenario is arithmetic exposure, not a forecast, and it does not assume default.

### Overall credit view

Overall, United Airlines Holdings, Inc. presents an adequate business profile supported by scale, liquidity, lower debt and a loyalty income stream, but credit quality is constrained by unhedged fuel, high capital intensity and rising labor cost. Cash-flow durability appears adequate to weak because free cash flow fell to USD 1,116 million over twelve months and underlying margin has fallen. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on liquidity, the extended revolver, positive rating momentum and market access for the 2029 principal. The primary downside path is fuel staying above fares while labor and aircraft costs keep rising. Further analysis would require the debt documents, covenant coverage figures, peer comparisons and a forward model. Fundamental credit synthesis completed. Top risk: unhedged fuel cost against fares, feeding weak free cash flow ahead of the 2029 maturities.
